topics.title: What is System Design?
objectives: Turn a product idea into components and responsibilities.
Trace a request and identify a failure boundary.

sections.title: Design starts with a user need
sections.text: System design is the process of choosing how software components cooperate to meet a concrete need under explicit constraints. Start with what a user must accomplish, the data that must survive, and the conditions the system must tolerate. A list of fashionable tools is not a design.

sections.title: Example: a shared reading list
sections.text: Assume a small team saves article URLs and reads the same list. The browser sends an authenticated request to an API. The API checks membership, validates the URL, and writes an item to a database. A background worker may fetch a page title after the write. The synchronous path should succeed even if that optional title fetch is slow.

sections.title: Define boundaries
sections.text: The client owns interaction, the API owns permission checks and business rules, and the database owns durable storage constraints. A request crosses boundaries where latency or failure can occur. A database timeout is different from a rejected permission check: communicate the outcome clearly and avoid telling the user a write succeeded before it is durable.

sections.title: Choose the smallest defensible baseline
sections.text: For this example, one deployable API and a relational database are a reasonable starting point. More services introduce deployment, coordination and observability work. If title enrichment becomes expensive, a separate worker isolates it, but introduces queue operations and delayed results. State the conditions that would justify the change.

sections.title: Failure exercise
sections.text: If a save times out after the database commits, a retry can duplicate the item. Propose a unique constraint or idempotency key and explain which duplicate the rule prevents. Consider the cost of rejecting two intentional saves of the same URL.

lesson.diagramCaption: Request path for a hypothetical reading-list application. Optional enrichment can run after the durable write.
lesson.example:
POST /lists/42/items
Authorization: <existing session>
{ "url": "https://example.com/article" }

201 Created only after the item is stored.
A retry must use an explicit duplicate policy.
lesson.exercise: Draw the reading-list architecture. Add the membership check, one timeout, and a safe retry policy. Explain why you chose synchronous or asynchronous title enrichment.
takeaways: Assign data and behavior to clear owners.
Explain failure behavior before adding scale.

quiz.question: Which decision belongs in the baseline design?
options: Choose five services before estimating demand.
Specify what happens if a write commits but its response is lost.
quiz.explanation: The response can be lost after a durable write. The design needs an explicit retry and duplicate policy.

topics.title: HLD vs LLD
objectives: Distinguish system boundaries from class boundaries.
Connect an HLD decision to an LLD contract.
Evaluate how a contract behaves under concurrent requests.

sections.title: Two views of the same system
sections.text: High-level design (HLD) describes services, data stores, communication paths, deployment boundaries and system-wide trade-offs. Low-level design (LLD) describes the internal responsibilities, interfaces, data structures and invariants that make a component correct. The boundary is a useful working distinction rather than a universal standard.

sections.title: HLD example: reserving seats
sections.text: A hypothetical booking system has a client, booking API and inventory database. The HLD explains which component owns seat availability, how users authenticate, and how the system responds when a dependency fails. A queue can handle email after a confirmed booking; it must not become a substitute for an atomic reservation decision.

sections.title: LLD example: the reservation contract
sections.text: Inside the booking component, ReservationService coordinates a repository and a clock. The repository exposes tryReserve(seatId, userId, expiresAt), with an atomic guarantee that at most one unexpired reservation owns a seat. A separate payment operation has its own retry policy. Interfaces express these promises; class diagrams alone do not enforce them.

sections.title: Where the views meet
sections.text: An HLD choice to run multiple booking instances means an in-memory lock in one process cannot prevent a second instance from reserving the same seat. The LLD must use a shared atomic operation, transaction or appropriate concurrency control. Test two callers competing for the same seat and specify the losing result.

sections.title: Trade-offs and change
sections.text: A single booking component can keep related rules together. Splitting inventory and booking creates distributed failure cases that require a carefully designed protocol. Decompose when independent scaling, ownership or deployment benefits justify that added coordination.

lesson.diagramCaption: HLD shows the network boundaries. LLD defines the atomic repository contract within the booking API.
lesson.exercise: Sketch the HLD and interfaces for seat reservation. Write three test cases: two concurrent callers, an expired hold, and a repeated request. Explain which layer enforces each invariant.
takeaways: LLD makes contracts and invariants concrete.
Concurrency assumptions must agree across both views.

quiz.question: Two API instances reserve the same seat. What is sufficient?
options: A shared atomic reservation rule in the inventory owner.
quiz.explanation: Separate process locks do not coordinate with each other. The seat owner needs a shared atomic rule.

topics.title: Functional and non-functional requirements
objectives: Separate required behavior from quality targets.
Write measurable latency and availability objectives.
Identify assumptions and exclusions before designing.

sections.title: Behavior and qualities
sections.text: Functional requirements describe what a system does: create a list, add an item, or reject an unauthorized request. Non-functional requirements describe measurable qualities or constraints: latency, availability, durability, privacy, operational cost or deployment limitations. Both affect architecture; security requirements often contain behavior as well as quality constraints.

sections.title: Make the scope testable
sections.text: For a hypothetical reading-list service, include creating lists, adding URLs and viewing lists shared with a user. Exclude public discovery and automated article summarization from the first design. State whether two items with the same URL are allowed. These choices prevent the system from silently growing beyond the problem.

sections.title: Turn adjectives into measurements
sections.text: Fast is ambiguous. An illustrative target could be: 95% of successful list-read requests complete within 300 ms, measured at the API edge over a rolling seven-day window for lists with at most 100 items. This is an assumed design target, not a measured result. Define the request population, percentile, observation point and window.

sections.title: Availability and durability differ
sections.text: A service can be reachable while losing data, or preserve data while temporarily rejecting requests. An illustrative availability objective might be 99.9% successful eligible requests over 30 days. Define which requests are eligible and how errors count. Separately state what a confirmed write promises and the backup or recovery expectations.

sections.title: Estimate before choosing capacity
sections.text: Assume 10,000 daily active users, each making 20 reads per day. That is 200,000 reads/day, or about 2.31 reads/second averaged across 86,400 seconds. A hypothetical 10× peak is about 23.1 reads/second. Average and peak estimates are planning assumptions; validate them with measurements. A read count alone does not establish storage, write load or response size.

sections.title: Trade-offs and review
sections.text: A stricter latency target may require indexes or caching, but cached shared-list data can become stale after permission changes. A tighter durability target may increase write latency and infrastructure cost. Record the decision, the acceptable failure behavior and a metric that would cause you to revisit it.

lesson.diagramCaption: Trace each design decision to a requirement and a way to evaluate it.
lesson.example:
Assumptions:
10,000 users/day × 20 reads/user = 200,000 reads/day
200,000 / 86,400 ≈ 2.31 reads/second (average)
10 × average ≈ 23.1 reads/second (assumed peak)

These are estimates, not production measurements.
lesson.exercise: Write three functional requirements and three measurable quality targets for the reading-list service. Add a load estimate, two exclusions and one trade-off. Distinguish assumptions from observed data.
takeaways: Specify units, percentiles and measurement windows.
Separate service availability from data durability.

quiz.question: Which is a measurable quality target?
options: The app should feel very fast.
95% of eligible reads finish within 300 ms at the API edge over seven days.
quiz.explanation: The target states a population, percentile, unit, observation point and window.
